For a finite convex line restriction $\varphi$ bounded below on the positive ray, suppose $\varphi'(0)=a<0$. Choose $\sigma=(c_1+c_2)/2$ and set $\psi(t)=\varphi(t)-\sigma at$. Its derivative at zero is $(1-\sigma)a<0$, while the lower bound on $\varphi$ makes $\psi(t)\to+\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$. Choose a compact interval $[0,M]$ whose interior contains a minimizer $z>0$ of $\psi$, with $\psi(z)<\psi(0)$. Then
\[
 \varphi(z)<\varphi(0)+\sigma az<\varphi(0)+c_1az.
\]
Continuity preserves strict Armijo on an interval immediately to the right of $z$. For each $t$ in a sufficiently small such interval, minimality and convexity give
\[
 \varphi'(t)\ge\frac{\varphi(t)-\varphi(z)}{t-z}\ge\sigma a>c_2a
\]
whenever the scalar derivative exists. Thus there is a nonempty open interval of strict Armijo points whose actual scalar derivatives satisfy strict weak Wolfe. If full-space nondifferentiability occurs at only finitely many positive ray times, choose a point in that interval outside this finite set; its actual full gradient gives a differentiable acceptable step. This is the proved tilted-minimum construction, replacing the earlier first-right-derivative-threshold route. It applies to finite affine absolute-value/hinge sums and suitable Euclidean residual sums through their proved full-space bad-ray-set finiteness. It gives existence, not a trial-complexity guarantee for every implementation.
